# Exploring qpAdm / qpGraph models

I think this particular mini project might be---out of every other
case study idea on offer---the most impactful for you if you're a
research in ancient DNA population genomics.

Both qpAdm and qpGraph techniques form a core component of nearly
every single impactful ancient DNA paper. Yet, a lot of research
work has been poured ([one
paper](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/217/4/iyaa045/6070149),
[another
paper](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/228/1/iyae110/7714968),
[yet another
paper](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/230/1/iyaf047/8102970))
into delineating in which situations qpAdm works and --- much more
often --- when it either fails to work or it's significantly
misinterpreted.

If you work with qpAdm, you're aware of many assumptions and
recommendations that are made, but those are rarely backed by
rigorous modeling and simulation.

**In this case study, I would encourage you to take some qpAdm /
qpGraph models you have inferred in the past (or some foundational
models infered in the literature relevant for your work), program
them in the form of parametrized _slendr_ models, and experiment
with how robust your conclusions are to some of the assumptions
made.**

**You already know that _slendr_ allows exporting data in the form
of EIGENSTRAT files via the function `ts_eigenstrat()` (as
introduced [in recipes in this
chapter](haplotype-methods.html#exercise-converting-tree-sequences-to-other-genotype-formats))
which means that connecting _slendr_ simulation scripts with the
[ADMIXTOOLS2](https://uqrmaie1.github.io/admixtools/index.html)
software in R is extremely straightforward.**
